lessons.title: Case Study: Tata Steel Through a Full Commodity Cycle

body.text: In twelve years, Tata Steel went from three straight years of losses to a record ₹41,749 crore profit and back to a loss. Its best single year produced almost half of all the profit it earned in the entire period. That is what a deep cyclical looks like in real numbers.

children.text: Everything in this chapter so far, operating leverage, financial leverage, spreads, the supply cycle, and the cost curve, shows up in one company's annual reports. Tata Steel is India's best-known steel maker, a Nifty 50 constituent, and owner of large operations in both India and Europe. Its consolidated numbers from FY15 to FY26 cover a bust, a recovery, a pandemic, a super-boom, another bust, and another recovery. Here is the whole cycle, phase by phase.

events.title: Corus acquisition
events.description: Tata Steel buys Anglo-Dutch steelmaker Corus, adding large European capacity and significant debt. This European business shapes the consolidated cycle for the next two decades.

events.title: Global steel glut
events.description: Chinese steel exports surge as its domestic demand slows. Global prices collapse. In February 2016, India imposes a minimum import price on many steel products to protect domestic producers.

events.title: Bhushan Steel bought through insolvency
events.description: Tata Steel's subsidiary acquires a 72.65% stake in Bhushan Steel under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, with ₹35,200 crore paid towards its financial creditors. Borrowings rise.

events.title: European joint venture blocked
events.description: The European Commission prohibits the planned merger of Tata Steel's and thyssenkrupp's European flat steel businesses, leaving Tata Steel with its loss-prone European operations.

events.title: Post-pandemic super-cycle
events.description: Stimulus-driven demand, supply disruptions, and the Russia-Ukraine war push global steel prices to record levels. Tata Steel earns record profits and cuts borrowings sharply.

events.title: Export duty on steel
events.description: The government imposes a 15% export duty on many steel products to cool domestic prices, hurting export realisations until it is withdrawn in November.

events.title: UK restructuring deal
events.description: Tata Steel agrees with the UK government on a £1.25 billion investment, including a £500 million government grant, to replace Port Talbot's blast furnaces with an electric arc furnace. Large impairment and restructuring charges follow, driving the FY24 consolidated loss.

events.title: Gradual recovery
events.description: Operating margins rebuild from 10% to 15%, and net profit recovers to ₹10,886 crore in FY26, still about a quarter of the FY22 peak.

children.text: Phase 1, FY15 to FY17: The Bust

Sales fell almost 27% in one year, from ₹1,39,504 crore in FY15 to ₹1,01,965 crore in FY16, as global prices collapsed. With blast furnaces, employees, and depreciation costing the same, operating profit turned negative in FY16. Borrowings of over ₹80,000 crore meant interest of more than ₹4,000 crore a year kept running regardless. Three consecutive loss years followed. This is operating leverage and financial leverage working together, exactly as Lesson 1 of this chapter described.
Phase 2, FY18 to FY21: Recovery, Debt, and a Pandemic

Prices recovered and OPM climbed to 17% in FY18 and 19% in FY19. But the Bhushan Steel acquisition pushed borrowings to a peak of ₹1,16,328 crore by FY20, just as demand weakened before the pandemic. Operating profit fell 40% in FY20 and net profit shrank to ₹1,174 crore. Then FY21 surprised: despite lockdowns, steel prices rebounded in the second half, OPM returned to 19%, and the company generated ₹44,327 crore of operating cash flow, which it used to cut borrowings to ₹88,501 crore.

body.title: Read the FY18 Number Carefully
body.question: Tata Steel's consolidated net profit was ₹17,743 crore in FY18 but only ₹9,122 crore in FY19, even though operating profit rose from ₹21,433 crore to ₹29,318 crore. What is the most likely explanation?
options: FY18 net profit was boosted by large non-operating items, visible in other income of ₹10,898 crore, so the operating profit line gives a truer picture of the business
The company paid a very large dividend in FY19
body.explanation: Operating profit rose strongly in FY19, so the business improved. FY18's other income of ₹10,898 crore, compared with ₹1,524 crore in FY19, flattered that year's bottom line. In cyclicals especially, exceptional gains and losses can distort net profit, so always check operating profit and OPM alongside it.

children.text: FY22 is operating leverage running in reverse, in the shareholder's favour. Sales rose 55.9%. Operating profit more than doubled, up 108%. Net profit grew 5.1 times, from ₹8,190 crore to ₹41,749 crore. OPM hit 26%. To its credit, management used the windfall to bring borrowings down to ₹75,561 crore, the lowest level in this 12-year window. Anyone extrapolating FY22 into the future, however, was about to be disappointed.

body.title: Tata Steel Consolidated Operating Profit Margin (OPM %)

children.text: Phase 4, FY23 to FY24: The Bust Returns

In FY23, sales were almost exactly flat at ₹2,43,353 crore. Yet operating profit halved and net profit fell 81%. How can revenue stay flat while profit collapses? Because steel prices cooled while coking coal and energy costs, driven up by the Russia-Ukraine war, stayed high. The spread shrank, which is precisely the price-versus-cost squeeze from Lesson 2. The export duty from May to November 2022 added pressure. In FY24, European losses and the impairment and restructuring charges tied to closing Port Talbot's blast furnaces pushed the consolidated result to a ₹4,910 crore loss.

body.title: Measure the Squeeze
body.prompt: Tata Steel's consolidated operating profit fell from ₹63,490 crore in FY22 to ₹22,248 crore in FY24. By what percentage did it fall? Enter the size of the fall as a positive number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (22,248 - 63,490) / 63,490 × 100 = -65.0%. Over the same two years, sales fell only 6.1%, from ₹2,43,959 crore to ₹2,29,171 crore. A single-digit revenue decline wiping out almost two thirds of operating profit is the spread and operating leverage acting together.

children.text: Two Businesses in One Stock: India vs Europe

Switch Screener.in from the consolidated view to the standalone view and you see mainly the Indian business. Standalone Tata Steel stayed profitable in every year from FY15 to FY26, including the years the consolidated company lost money. It was still clearly cyclical: standalone net profit fell 55.5% from ₹33,011 crore in FY22 to ₹14,685 crore in FY23, and its OPM ranged from 19% to 40%. But it never went into the red. The difference is the cost curve.

body.title: Why the Indian and European Operations Behave So Differently

columns.label: India operations
points: Captive iron ore mines supply a large share of raw material needs
Relatively low labour and conversion costs
Sits low on the global cost curve, so stays profitable in troughs

columns.label: European operations
points: Buys most iron ore and coking coal from the market
Higher labour, energy, and carbon compliance costs
Mature, slow-growing demand with strong import competition
Sits higher on the cost curve, so losses appear quickly when prices fall

body.title: The Cost Curve Advantage
body.textWithBlank: A major reason Tata Steel's Indian operations stayed profitable through downturns is their access to captive ___ mines, which keeps raw material costs low.
body.explanation: Owning iron ore mines protects the Indian business from the full swing of global raw material prices, placing it lower on the cost curve than producers that buy ore on the open market.

body.text: Tata Steel split each ₹10 share into ten ₹1 shares in July 2022. Screener.in shows per-share figures such as EPS on a split-adjusted basis, but older news articles and charts may quote pre-split prices. Always confirm you are comparing prices on the same basis before calculating returns or P/E ratios.

body.title: April 2022: What Would You Have Done?
body.scenario: It is April 2022. Tata Steel has just reported record FY22 net profit of ₹41,749 crore, up 5.1 times in a year. Borrowings are the lowest in years, the stock trades at a single-digit P/E, and brokerage reports talk about a steel super-cycle driven by infrastructure and supply disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine war. A colleague says it is the cheapest quality stock in the Nifty 50.
body.prompt: Using everything from this chapter, what warning signs would you have raised, and what would you have checked?
body.modelAnswer: Several deep-cyclical warning signs were visible. OPM at 26% was the highest in the company's recent history and far above its long-run range, which signals peak spreads rather than a new normal. FY22 alone was on track to be a very large share of the decade's profit, so the single-digit P/E was calculated on earnings unlikely to repeat. Coking coal and energy costs were rising sharply, threatening the spread even if steel prices held. The European business sat high on the cost curve and had a history of losses in downturns. The right checks: where OPM and EBITDA per tonne sat against the 10-year range, what Chinese steel exports and global prices were doing, what the input cost trend looked like, and what net profit would be at mid-cycle margins rather than peak margins. The lower debt was genuinely positive, but it reduced the risk of a crisis; it did not stop profits falling 81% the next year.

body.title: Build Your Own Cycle Case Study
steps: Pick a cyclical you own or follow, such as JSW Steel, Hindalco, or a cement company
Open its consolidated Profit and Loss and Balance Sheet on Screener.in and copy 10 to 12 years of Sales, Operating Profit, OPM %, Net Profit, and Borrowings
Mark the loss years, the peak year, and the trough years
Divide the history into phases: bust, recovery, peak, and bust again
For each phase, look up two or three events from annual reports or news that explain the move
Compare consolidated and standalone views to see whether one business drives most of the volatility
Calculate what share of total profit came from the single best year
Run the Chapter 1 scorecard and write a one-line verdict

points: Tata Steel posted losses in 4 of 12 years from FY15 to FY26, and FY22 alone delivered 48% of the period's total net profit
In FY22, a 55.9% sales rise turned into a 108% jump in operating profit and a 5.1 times rise in net profit
Between FY22 and FY24, sales fell just 6.1% but operating profit fell 65%, because the spread between steel prices and input costs collapsed
Debt amplified the FY15 to FY17 bust; paying down debt in the FY21 and FY22 boom reduced crisis risk but could not stop the earnings cycle
The low-cost Indian business stayed profitable throughout, while the higher-cost European business drove the consolidated losses
Check operating profit and OPM alongside net profit, since exceptional items can distort a cyclical's bottom line in either direction

body.text: Financial figures are annual consolidated and standalone data as displayed on Screener.in at the time of writing and may be restated in later filings, particularly after group mergers. Event descriptions summarise public reports. This case study is for education only and is not a recommendation to buy or sell Tata Steel or any other security.
